title: Here’s the latest.
text:
Live Updates: U.S. Hiring Picks Up and Unemployment Falls
U.S. employers hired at a vigorous pace in October, adding 165,000 jobs. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent.
Monthly change in jobs
Latest
Hiring was unexpectedly strong in October, when employers added workers at a vigorous pace.
Employers added 165,000 jobs last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday, and the unemployment rate dropped to 4.1 percent. Job gains for August and September were revised upward by a total of 84,000 positions. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent compared with the same time last year.
The report reaffirmed the general picture of the labor market as healthy. Employers have broadly continued to hire despite President Trump’s volatile tariff policy, the war in Iran that has cranked up energy price and uncertainty over artificial intelligence. Businesses have held onto their workers, keeping layoffs at historically low levels. And employees have been reluctant to leave their jobs.
Here’s what to know:
Solid, not strong: Employers have been adding workers at a slow but steady pace for months. The unemployment rate has stayed low, hovering in a narrow range for the last two years. The robust October report underscored the labor market’s resilience but did not change this overall picture.
Bad vibes: Though the labor market has remained solid, people who are looking for work, including recent college graduates, have found limited opportunities. And even those who do have jobs have been losing leverage, as wage growth has slowed and inflation has continued to erode their spending power. Those factors could help explain why so many Americans are feeling dour about the economy.
A.I. jitters: One big question hanging over the labor market is the impact of artificial intelligence. So far, the technology does not appear to be leading to widespread job losses. But there are some indications that the rise of the technology is depressing hiring, particularly for entry-level positions in sectors including financial services and information.
Green shoots? There have been some tentative signs that the labor market may be on the verge of perking up. The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey this week showed that the quits rate rose in September, a sign that workers may be feeling more confident in their ability to get new jobs.
Stocks haven’t reacted much to today’s jobs numbers, with futures on the S&P 500 up 0.1 percent. Treasury yields are up slightly.
The monthly jobs numbers are volatile and subject to revision, so economists caution against reading too much into any one report. But between the strong October numbers and the upward adjustments to prior months, this report makes the recent trend in job growth look meaningfully better. Employers have added an average of 137,000 jobs per month over the past three months. Before this morning’s numbers, the three-month average stood at just 51,000 jobs.
Those numbers have slightly pushed up expectations for rate increases next year, which had been falling as markets sold off in recent weeks. Investors are betting on the Fed next raising rates in January, with another quarter point rate increase to come after that as well.
White-collar sectors mostly added jobs last month. Professional and business services — a broad category that includes accountants, travel agents and many other office jobs — added 70,000 jobs. The financial sector added 7,000, while employment in the information sector fell slightly. Weakness in those sectors in recent months has contributed to concerns that artificial intelligence is eroding white-collar jobs. But the October data suggests some strength.
White-collar jobs saw some growth
This jobs report will affirm the Fed’s view that the labor market is on solid footing and that officials can afford to keep their attention trained on taming inflation, which has accelerated this year. That is likely to translate to additional interest rate increases unless there is a substantial sell-off across financial markets that is extreme enough to begin to weigh on growth.
Today’s jobs data reinforces a point that even some Republicans had made before the party’s election rout: There were bright spots in the economy, including stable hiring, but none were enough to change the minds of voters hammered by persistent inflation.
Despite the pickup in monthly jobs growth and a slight decline in the unemployment rate, wage growth has stayed relatively subdued. Average hourly earnings picked up a bit in October, rising 0.4 percent for the month or 3.1 percent compared to the same time last year.
Totals for August and September were both revised up, by a combined 84,000 jobs.
Stocks were slightly higher ahead of the numbers with futures on the S&P 500, which allow investors to bet on the market before exchanges open for trading, up 0.3 percent.
The numbers are out! U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent.
One aspect of the labor market that has fortified the Fed’s gradual approach to raising rates is the fact that wage growth has stayed subdued. That suggests the labor market is not contributing to inflationary pressures. Any indication that this dynamic is changing could alter the Fed’s pace of tightening.
Slowing economic growth coming from the expanding artificial intelligence industry is likely to take the pressure off inflation. This would give the central bank more ability to focus on the labor market, prompting investors to dial down expectations for how quickly the Fed will raise interest rates.
It didn’t get much attention because of the election news, but the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Tuesday released data showing an increase in both job openings and hiring in September. Layoffs, which have been consistently low, fell further, while more workers voluntarily quit their jobs, a sign of confidence. None of the numbers suggested that the labor market has broken definitively out of the “low-hire, low-fire” stasis that it has been in for the past couple years. But the report did provide some encouraging hints that activity could be starting to pick up.
A strong jobs report could give the sluggish housing market a much-needed shot in the arm, said Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, a real estate marketplace. Sales of existing homes fell 2.2 percent in September from the year before, as inflation worries and elevated mortgage rates weighed on buyers. “A more dynamic labor market with real wage growth is sorely needed for buying power and demand,” Mr. Krimmel said.
So long as the labor market stays on solid footing, officials at the Fed feel confident that they can afford to focus their attention on taming inflation, which has overshot the 2 percent target for nearly six years. They’ve adopted a gradual approach, which so far appears to be translating to an every-other-meeting cadence.
Officials raised rates in September, held them steady in October and several policymakers have indicated their support for a December move. That was before markets sold off sharply in the wake of the midterm elections, a move that prompted questions about how much more the Fed will lift borrowing costs.
On Tuesday, voters across the country swept out incumbent Republicans in large part because of their frustration about the state of the economy. Today, barring a surprise, the Bureau of Labor Statistics will report that the unemployment rate remained below 4.5 percent, where it’s been for a record five years.
At first glance, those two facts may seem hard to reconcile. But the labor market isn’t as strong as the unemployment rate suggests. Yes, most people have jobs and layoffs are low. But hiring has been sluggish, leaving workers with little leverage. As a result, wage growth has slowed and has lagged behind inflation for much of this year. Economists will be watching today’s data for any hint of a pickup.
The Federal Reserve has settled on raising interest rates gradually as it seeks to tame inflation. That suggests the central bank will lift borrowing costs again in December, and at least one more time in 2027.
An accelerating labor market, or one that falters, could alter that approach.
The labor market has not contributed to the inflation problem confronting the Fed, a dynamic that was affirmed when data for October was released on Friday. Monthly jobs growth was strong and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent, but wage growth remains relatively muted. Average hourly earnings picked up a bit in October, rising 0.4 percent for the month. Compared to the same time last year, it is up 3.1 percent.
This backdrop is a welcome one for policymakers at the Fed. It suggests they can afford to focus primarily on curbing inflation, which has overshot the central bank’s 2 percent target for nearly six years.
The primary drivers of inflation include the war with Iran, which has unleashed an energy shock that has sharply lifted oil prices, as well as a spending boom by technology companies building out their artificial intelligence abilities.
Shares in those companies have come under pressure after Democrats’ sweeping victory in this week’s midterm elections that gave them firm control of both chambers of Congress. The prospects of heightened A.I. scrutiny and a regulatory crackdown prompted a steep slide in U.S. stocks, with the S&P 500 notching its worst daily decline on Thursday in more than a year.
Fed officials are tracking gyrations in the stock market and the trajectory of U.S. government bond yields, which together influence the availability of credit in the economy.
Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, acknowledged at the bank’s policy meeting last week that those financial conditions had become tighter. But he said he was “unwilling and unable to call them tight.”
Mr. Warsh appeared to welcome the move, saying that it helped “in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.”
Mr. Warsh made clear that the Fed’s goal wasn’t “to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work.” That suggests the bar is relatively high for the Fed to jettison its gradual approach to raising rates. It would take fresh evidence that price pressures are intensifying, and perhaps beginning to stem from the labor market. That would very likely necessitate a much more aggressive response from the Fed, either in terms of the pace of further rate increases or the total amount it would eventually deliver.
How stocks are trading in the United States
Investors faced another volatile trading session on Friday, with U.S. stock futures pointing to a rebound in technology shares that would reverse some of the punishing losses from the day before, capping the end of a turbulent week.
The fallout from Wall Street’s worst day in nearly two years reverberated around the world, as growing concerns over runaway spending on artificial intelligence dragged down technology shares. Markets in Asia were hit hard on Friday, but as trading got underway in Europe the tide began to turn.
Futures for the S&P 500 signaled that the benchmark index would rise slightly when official trading opens in New York. The Nasdaq, which was at the forefront of the rout on Thursday, was set to open more than 1 percent higher, driven by a bounce in chip makers, like Nvidia.
A rally on Friday would continue the week’s wrenching volatility, which saw stocks rise as the U.S. midterm election results rolled in, but then veer sharply lower as investors grappled with the prospects for the A.I. investment boom after the Democrats’ landslide victory. The shift in power in Congress led many analysts to suggest that stricter regulation of data centers could slow growth in states where the world’s largest tech companies are aggressively building out computing capacity.
Phillip Wool, head of research and portfolio management at Rayliant, an investment firm, said that even if a Congress controlled by Democrats wanted to take a tougher approach on A.I. companies, President Trump still held veto power. “At best, this is probably a stalemate, and it’s just going to bring more attention to some of the risks of A.I.,” he said.
Other market watchers said that the sell-off most likely represented traders resetting their positions as they assessed the implications of the U.S. elections, rather than an end to the A.I. investment cycle that had propelled markets higher for much of this year.
“While we could see a period of market indigestion following the election results, we do not think fundamentals justify a prolonged downturn,” said Mark Haefele, the chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, adding that corporate earnings remained resilient. But he warned that more spells of market volatility could be ahead.
The latest U.S. jobs report, due before the market opens on Friday, typically moves markets and will be another factor attracting investors’ attention.
Markets across Asia, which were closed during the worst of the selling on Wall Street, had a chaotic open to trading on Friday. The severity of the initial selling in South Korea triggered a 20-minute trading halt at the exchange in Seoul. The tech-heavy KOSPI plunged 6 percent by the end of the session, pulled down by the memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 sank about 6 percent, dropping the index into a bear market, defined as a 20 percent fall from its recent peak. Shares of SoftBank, a major investor in OpenAI and a proxy for investor sentiment on A.I., plunged 11 percent.
In Europe, the Stoxx 600, a broad index that tracks the region’s largest companies, shed more than 1 percent. All of the continent’s major markets, in Frankfurt, Paris, London and beyond, posted declines, but the moves were less severe than elsewhere, since European indexes are less influenced by technology companies.
In fact, some of Europe’s biggest tech companies posted gains on Friday. ASML, Infineon and STMicroelectronics were among the stocks that rose between 2 and 4 percent.
For Mohit Kumar, a strategist at Jefferies, the recent turmoil after the U.S. midterms was not a sign of the unwinding of the A.I. trade. “One could argue that having more guardrails makes A.I. investment more sustainable in the medium term,” he wrote in a research note.
Within an hour of Microsoft’s announcement of buyouts last week, employees rushed to an internal site to see whether they had been offered one. So many people were checking at once that employees speculated on the company’s internal social network that the site had buckled under the traffic.
The offer, extended to about 60,000 employees, or more than a quarter of Microsoft’s work force, was the largest in the company’s history. It was also the company’s second buyout this year, and another shock to a work force grappling with big changes brought on by artificial intelligence.
For years, Microsoft occupied a distinct position among the tech industry’s biggest companies. While its pay packages often lagged behind Silicon Valley rivals like Google and Meta, employees said, the company countered with strong benefits and a reputation for stability. As recently as September, Forbes ranked Microsoft the world’s best employer for the third straight year.
But the tech industry’s A.I. race is upending many workplaces, Microsoft included. The buyout offer, said six Microsoft employees who spoke on the condition of anonymity, landed on workers strained by mounting expectations to use A.I., stagnant pay and a growing sense that their jobs were no longer secure.
Though Microsoft is doing better financially than most of its peers, it is clearly shifting its spending priorities. Two days after the buyouts were announced, the Redmond, Wash., company reported a 32 percent jump in quarterly profit, to $36.6 billion, on revenue of $92.3 billion. Its capital spending, largely on data centers, rose 30 percent to $45.2 billion, and the company said it expected to spend roughly $170 billion this year.
The fear among many workers now is what comes next, and some have begun organizing. Before the buyout offer, a group of current and former employees circulated an open letter among colleagues accusing the company of pursuing A.I. with a “speed-at-all-costs” ethos. It called on Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how A.I. is built and used, and to stop tying A.I. use to rewards or reprimands.
Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice president and chief people officer, said the buyouts were meant to give employees who might be ready for something new “choice and agency.” She said the buyouts were not related to how A.I. was changing work. (A Microsoft spokeswoman said “maintenance timing,” rather than a traffic surge, had briefly delayed the release of some buyout offers on the internal site.)
Ms. Coleman also did not rule out future layoffs.
Employees offered a buyout have until Dec. 9 to decide, and those who accept will leave on Dec. 31. They will receive a minimum of eight weeks of base pay, and the size of the payment varies by job level and tenure.
The offer followed a string of cuts that had already shaken employees. Microsoft laid off 10,000 workers in 2023, and more than 15,000 in 2025. This spring, about 8,600 U.S. employees were offered a retirement-age buyout, and about 30 percent accepted it. This summer, the company cut about 4,800 more jobs. Microsoft’s head count in June was 223,000, down 5,000 from a year earlier.
This time, Microsoft said it expected less than 5 percent of the 60,000 employees offered a buyout to take it.
Some employees have already signed the offer, including one who has been at Microsoft for nearly a decade. She was her family’s main earner and worried about the job market, she said. But years of pressure to use unreliable A.I. tools, the constant threat of layoffs and what she saw as a widening gap between the company’s stated values and its actions made staying feel worse. Colleagues urged her to stay, she said, because they would have to absorb her work.
Others are staying, at least for now, some by choice and some because they feel they have none. A senior software engineer who has worked at Microsoft for more than five years said he wanted to stay to try to improve the company. He said a recent squeeze on pay, the push to use A.I. and now the buyouts had left far more of his colleagues feeling expendable.
Several employees said that merit raises this year had been unusually small, in some cases less than 1 percent, and that managers had described rewards budgets as tight. At a company town hall last month, a question about how executives balanced spending more than $100 billion a year on A.I. against flat rewards for the workers carrying out that strategy drew more than 80 reactions, roughly twice as many as most other questions seen by The New York Times.
Ms. Coleman said Microsoft was trying to stay competitive on pay while it remained “a company that has to think about our operating expense and our capital expense.”
The tension had begun to show up in pay in other ways, too, employees said. Gretchen Thomas, 57, a design leader, left Microsoft in September after five years because the pressure grew steadily heavier, she said, including shifting priorities and faster deadlines.
“I just can’t believe how grim it’s gotten just in the last three years,” she said.
This year, Ms. Thomas’s raise and bonus were in line with those of her colleagues. But her manager had reduced her stock award, typically the most valuable part of a Microsoft employee’s pay, because, according to a memo seen by The Times, she did “not consistently” show speed, urgency and willingness to experiment, including with A.I.
Ms. Coleman declined to discuss individual pay decisions, but said the company encouraged employees to experiment and use its tools. “Of course some of that includes A.I.,” she said.
For those who stay, employees said, the bigger worry is the work left behind. All of the employees said that they did not expect departing colleagues to be replaced, and that the remaining staff would absorb their work. Ms. Coleman said Microsoft had thousands of jobs open but acknowledged the company needed to make “some shifts in the work force.”
(The Times has sued Microsoft and OpenAI, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied the suit’s claims.)
The day after the buyout announcement, a group of teams in one of Microsoft’s software organizations gathered at a Dave & Buster’s for an event to raise morale that had been planned for a month.
Before the food came out, a five-year engineer who was at the event recalled, a manager stood on a chair, acknowledged that all the attendees were refreshing their email and weighing the buyout offer, and urged them to set it aside and celebrate the work they had done.
At his table, the engineer said, no one talked about anything else.
Stocks had their worst day in nearly two years as investors’ concerns about weaknesses in the A.I. industry re-emerged after Democratic midterm victories raised the prospect of tighter regulation.
The S&P 500 fell 4.4 percent on Thursday, marking the most severe drop for the index since April 2025, when President Trump unveiled sweeping global tariffs.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.5 percent, putting the index into correction, defined as a drop of 10 percent or more from its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a benchmark for the industry, tumbled over 12 percent. That index has fallen over 30 percent since the beginning of October and is almost 40 percent below its peak in June.
After the Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate, the market initially rallied on Wednesday, as gridlock in Washington has broadly been welcomed by investors because it reduces the likelihood of new rules and laws being imposed on businesses.
But by Thursday morning, concerns about the midterms ushering in a period of heightened scrutiny of A.I. compounded the fears of runaway spending and rising debt at tech firms that had been swirling in the market for weeks.
Some analysts noted that Democrats had flipped key governorships in states that are becoming important hubs for data centers, and that this could create a meaningful roadblock to the A.I. build-out.
The declines gathered pace through the day, engulfing all sectors of the S&P 500. And as stocks tumbled, the 10-year Treasury note, seen as a haven during periods of market stress, rallied, meaning its yield fell, dropping to 4.83 percent, its lowest since September.
Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group, said the sell-off had become “exaggerated” as selling accelerated through the day. He predicted the market would recover.
“When you have a correction in a bull market they are typically short lived,” he said. “It’s ugly right now but we do think we will see a bounce back soon.”
Nasdaq Composite Index
How the tech-heavy index in the United States is trading
Thursday’s decline rekindled a sell-off that had paused in the immediate run-up to the election. That sell-off had intensified last week when tech giants like Meta and Amazon reported their quarterly results that included huge spending plans on A.I., amplifying concerns about how quickly these investments would result in increased profits.
On Thursday, some of the biggest losses occurred among the chip makers. Qualcomm, a large chipmaker, sank 9.5 percent on Thursday after the company dialed down its earnings forecast; it said high demand for chips was raising its own costs faster than it has been able to raise prices. The sharp stock move reflected broader concerns that supply bottlenecks created by the rush to build A.I. infrastructure could slow the industry’s growth, which means slowing the time it takes for investors to realize profits on their A.I. bets.
Arm Holdings, another chipmaker, fell 13.1 percent after reporting underwhelming revenue from its push into A.I.
Nvidia, a chip industry leader, dropped 9.3 percent, dragging its stock into negative territory for the year.
Shares of Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX fell sharply for a second day. The two companies are run by the world’s richest person — and Republican megadonor — and have come under particular focus after the elections, with potential investigations and regulatory scrutiny in store.
The stocks of some of the large “hyperscalers,” like Alphabet and Microsoft, fell less on Thursday than the broader market. Some analysts suggested that a slowdown in the race to build A.I infrastructure could favor these large, entrenched players, securing their dominant position and slowing the rapid pace of spending that has put pressure on their businesses.
“The underlying intuition is that a slower build out could be relatively favorable for those doing the spending, and potentially less so for those receiving it,” said Frank Flight, head of macro strategy at Citadel Securities.
Analysts broadly remained sanguine about the outlook for the stock market, expecting major indexes to rally once the current volatility subsides, though some expected choppy trading to continue through the end of the year.
Many saw the tech sell-off as part of the move out of some of the companies that have led the market higher and into the next cohort of companies to benefit from the adoption of the technology, such as health care companies and financials.
Many also noted that the S&P 500 has risen over the 12 months after every midterm election since the Second World War. The index remains 7.4 percent higher for the year.
“The valuations in some of these names had just got so frothy, it’s not a complete surprise that we are seeing this,” said Alan McKnight, chief investment officer at Regions Bank.
How stocks are trading in the United States
The U.S. trade deficit — a measure of the difference between what the country imports and what it exports — ticked downward slightly in September from the previous month but remained at relatively high levels, defying efforts by the Trump administration to shrink it.
The trade deficit in goods and services dropped to $105 billion in September, a 0.7 percent decrease from August. While the measure retreated slightly from a record high the prior month, it was still the second-largest monthly total since President Trump imposed his global tariffs in April 2025.
The metric has steadily ticked up in recent months, in part because companies are importing large shipments of expensive artificial intelligence chips and computers to fill new data centers.
In September, imports grew 1.2 percent from the prior month, to reach a record $426.6 billion, as the United States bought more computers and pharmaceuticals. Exports rose 1.9 percent from the previous month to $321.5 billion. That increase was driven by the exports of computers, crude oil and aircraft, as well as large orders of American soybeans placed by Chinese firms ahead of a U.S. visit by the Chinese president.
The high trade deficit has come as bad news for the Trump administration, which sees the metric as a sign of weakness in America’s manufacturing sector. Mr. Trump has tried to reduce the trade deficit by imposing hefty tariffs on many American imports.
But some economists have questioned whether the strategy would work, given generally high spending by U.S. consumers and the government.
They have also pointed out that the administration has largely exempted goods like pharmaceuticals and A.I. chips, which make up much of the value of U.S. imports, even as it imposes tariffs on everyday consumer products like furniture, toys and clothing.
The most notable impact of the tariffs so far appears to be that they have made trade much more volatile. After Mr. Trump’s election, businesses rushed to bring in large shipments ahead of tariffs going into effect, and the trade deficit surged.
The trade deficit then dropped sharply in April, after Mr. Trump imposed sweeping global tariffs. To avoid paying tariffs, companies continued to draw on packed warehouses and were able to import less for many months. But beginning this summer, the trade deficit began to steadily creep upward again.
The Trump administration has been planning to impose more tariffs on foreign products in the months to come, even as previously issued tariffs continue to face challenges in the courts.
It remains to be seen if Tuesday’s Democratic sweep will derail any of those plans. Mr. Trump’s tariffs came under fire during the campaigns from voters who blamed tariffs for adding to their higher cost of living.
Brad Setser, an economist at the Council on Foreign Relations, said voters’ cost-of-living concerns were actually driven more by the high price of gas, housing and medical care than tariffs. Still, price increases from tariffs were likely to be somewhat noticeable to shoppers, he said.
“If you’re going to Walmart and you’re surprised at the cost of some products, that is partly tariffs,” he said. “There’s an extent to which the tariffs have been designed to hit people shopping at Walmart and not people building data centers.”
Microsoft on Monday offered buyouts to a quarter of its work force, the latest effort by the company to rein in costs as it spends heavily on artificial intelligence.
Only a sliver of the 60,000 employees offered a buyout are expected to take it, the company said.
In a note to staff, Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s chief people officer, wrote that the buyout is part of the company’s efforts to give employees more control over their future and also “meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.”
The “time-limited, voluntary” program grew out of the company’s first ever buyouts earlier this year, she wrote. In April, Microsoft offered early retirement to 8,600 long-tenured U.S. employees, and about 30 percent accepted the packages and left over the summer. Microsoft said it heard from additional employees who would have taken the buyout if they had been eligible. That informed the company’s decision to create this new, expanded program.
Between 3 and 5 percent of tech industry employees typically accept buyout offers, Microsoft said.
Like its Big Tech peers, Microsoft has been cutting costs to plow money into the A.I. race. The company told investors to expect its capital spending, largely on data centers and the chips to fill them, to total about $190 billion in 2026.
Microsoft has already slightly shrunk its work force even as business has boomed. For several years, the company maintained a flat head count of about 228,000 employees.
But as of June 30, the end of its fiscal year, Microsoft’s work force had edged lower to 223,000 employees. Over that same fiscal year, Microsoft brought in $332 billion in revenue, up 18 percent from the previous year, and profit grew 31 percent to $134 billion.
In July, Microsoft announced it was cutting 4,800 jobs, particularly in its video game division. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Wednesday.
Monday’s buyout offer was widespread — available to vice president levels on down — and went to select teams in Canada, India, Britain and the United States. Some teams, such as sales and some in engineering, were excluded.
The terms of the offer were less generous than the retirement buyout, part of why the company thinks fewer people will take it. This new program provides the company’s standard severance package, which includes a minimum of eight weeks base pay, and steps up based on tenure. An employee’s last day would be Dec. 31.
Gena Pemberton is a Black woman who has spent her career diagnosing a way to move forward in corporate America.
She spent over two decades in leadership roles in accounting, operations and human resources at large companies such as Johnson & Johnson. But now, at 50, she is not sure what is next.
She was the chief inclusion and impact officer at Omnicom Health until the company eliminated her position in July 2025. She has been without full-time work ever since, despite applying to dozens of jobs per week and lowering her expectations on seniority and pay.
“I’ve never been unemployed for this long,” she said.
Ms. Pemberton is far from alone. Black professionals across the country have faced a triple whammy in the labor market in recent years.
The disappearance of diversity, equity and inclusion positions in big companies has heavily affected Black women; a federal government firing spree that eliminated hundreds of thousands of jobs had a heavy impact on Black workers, who are disproportionately represented on federal payrolls; and the slowdown in white-collar hiring rates has felt particularly acute for some Black businesspeople without elite networks as expansive as those of their white and Asian peers.
When unemployment for Black workers rises sharply, it can be an early signal of trouble for everyone. Rising joblessness among Black people and weak hiring rates in the business services sector are signals that the labor market is in worse shape than the overall 4.2 percent unemployment rate implies, said Jared Bernstein, who served as chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. Hiring, for example, is proceeding at a pace analogous to the sluggish years after the Great Recession, when overall unemployment was closer to 9 percent and Black unemployment was in the midteens.
“When the economy sniffles, Black unemployment catches a cold,” he said.
In 2025, Black women experienced far greater employment losses than other women, especially college graduates and public-sector workers, according to data analyzed by Valerie Wilson, an economist. And numbers from Revelio Labs, a work force analytics firm, show that U.S. employers have cut over 2,600 roles since 2023 with “diversity” or “D.E.I.” in the job titles or descriptions.
After spiking above 8 percent in November 2025, Black unemployment fell to 6 percent by August. Then, the latest jobs report showed that unemployment for Black people had jumped back to 7 percent in September — the fastest one-month increase since 2012, not counting the brief pandemic shock. The rate is almost double the 3.6 percent rate for white workers.
“It is definitely a cause for concern,” Kevin Hassett, the generally ebullient director of the White House National Economic Council, said in an interview with CNN.
Employment levels for Black women 20 and older have been volatile and declined to 10.3 million from a record high of around 10.7 million in 2023. Nursing, health care and other social assistance jobs have held up best for Black women, mirroring the picture in the broader labor market. But at one point, the decrease in employment for Black women constituted more than half of job losses for all women.
Employment levels for Black men have fallen, too, from a peak near 10 million in 2025, yet have recovered slightly since this spring. And while Black men have experienced a decline in manufacturing jobs, they have fared better than Black women in the “professional and business services” sector, gaining over 100,000 jobs on net. Black women have lost jobs in the sector.
Unemployment figures are based on a survey of households, and economists caution against reading too much into monthly changes. That is particularly true of the estimates for individual demographic groups, which are based on relatively small sample sizes.
Ms. Pemberton, who lost her job at Omnicom Health last year, may not even technically be counted as unemployed since she has been doing consulting work while searching for a full-time position. That income has, however, been comparatively patchy.
Under Labor Department guidelines, people are considered employed if they did any work during the middle of the month when the jobs survey is conducted. This includes part-time jobs as well as freelancing, gig or contract work.
The financial cliff Ms. Pemberton has experienced has caused a strain not felt since childhood, she said, when her parents were living paycheck to paycheck some years.
“I have pretty much gutted almost all my savings — not just my savings account, but now I’m tapping into my 401(k), which means my future is impacted,” Ms. Pemberton said. “I have been looking at jobs that are probably a lower title, and lower pay, because I’ve got to figure this out.”
Using 401(k) accounts for hardship withdrawals has more than doubled in recent years, driven partly by the long-term unemployed digging into their retirement savings for emergencies.
Vina Morris, president of the New York chapter of the National Black MBA Association, a nonprofit network, said people just looking at the headline Black unemployment rate underestimated how badly the situation had deteriorated since the early 2020s, when efforts to lift longstanding barriers to Black leadership in business were in vogue.
“We’ve lost partnerships,” Ms. Morris said, regarding corporate donors. “And we’ve lost funding.”
It does not help, Ms. Morris added, that artificial intelligence has clouded and clogged the job application process — and that, in response, many managers have returned to old-school hiring tactics: picking those who seem trustworthy via word of mouth from friends and social back channels.
“We’re not in many of those rooms, don’t always have many of those same friends,” she said.
President Trump, in his first term, frequently heralded the low rate of Black unemployment and, in his second term, argued that his strict immigration policies would benefit Black Americans by keeping out low-income immigrants stealing “Black jobs.” Economists, however, have said that there is little evidence to support that claim and that Black jobs have long included higher-income careers. They note that some of Mr. Trump’s policies, particularly the government job cuts, have hurt Black workers.
Melinda Emerson, an adjunct professor at Rutgers Business School who started a work force development company, said the federal government’s rollback of support for Black entrepreneurship and minority contractors had been an enormous hit to her community.
“It’s not just unemployment,” Ms. Emerson said.
She has seen many Black contractors in her network have their government contracts canceled, she said, while accountability measures like “scorecards” for the diversity of your vendor and client relationships have vanished in corporate America — all of which have caused sales for many proprietors of color to dry up.
Ms. Emerson accused the Trump administration of fomenting a negative culture about the professionalism of people of color. She argues that the government’s racially charged language — suggesting that diversity and excellence are at odds — has trickled down into corporate values and decisions.
“So many of our clients’ budgets have gotten slashed, so we just don’t have the opportunities that we used to,” she said.
Ms. Emerson has experienced a 50 percent decline in sales since 2023, nearly all of which she attributes to anti-D.E.I. sociopolitical winds. Some of the offered pay rates, she said, are barely higher than her team’s operational costs.
“When your biggest customer calls you,” Ms. Emerson explained, “and says, ‘Melinda, I have this project for you, and I know that we should be giving you $70,000 for this, but now I’ve got 20K, will you do it?’ I mean, come on — but those are the kind of conversations we’re having.”
Some labor market experts remain hopeful. Cantrell Dumas, a senior researcher at the Joint Center, a think tank focused on economic outcomes for Black Americans, saw reasons for optimism. Black labor force participation is relatively strong, and the reversal of Black unemployment from its earlier 2025 peak shows that things can turn around again.
“The problem is not that Black workers stopped looking for work,” Mr. Dumas said. “It was that more Black workers came into the labor market and the jobs weren’t there to meet them.”
Ms. Pemberton figures her next job will be connected to her earlier roles in financial analysis.
“It’s like nobody even wants to hear the acronym D.E.I. anymore,” she said.
